full_text:
Nasdaq ends over 1% lower as tech stocks take a hit on OpenAI revenue report
Investing.com-- U.S. stock futures were little changed Thursday night after Wall Street fell for a second straight session, as concerns over OpenAI's revenue outlook weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks and rising oil prices revived inflation worries.
S&P 500 Futures inched 0.1% higher to 7,825.25.0 points, while Nasdaq 100 Futures traded flat at 30,978.75 points by 20:26 ET (00:26 GMT). Dow Jones Futures traded 0.2% higher at 51,570.0 points.
In the regular session, the NASDAQ Composite fell 1.3% to 27,193.34, while the S&P 500 lost 0.5% to 7,765.36. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.1% to 51,231.64, outperforming the broader market as technology shares came under pressure.
The pullback came two days after the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 reached record closing highs, with investors also assessing the outlook for interest rates ahead of the start of the third-quarter earnings season.
The technology-heavy Nasdaq bore the brunt of the selloff after a Financial Times report said OpenAI had told investors its annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion at the end of September, below the $70 billion figure previously reported by media outlets.
The discrepancy stemmed from differences in how OpenAI and rival Anthropic account for sales through cloud partners, the FT reported. Anthropic includes revenue from partners such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, while OpenAI excludes those sales from its calculation, according to the report.
The figures raised questions about the scale of AI demand and the financial returns on heavy investment in computing infrastructure.
Chipmakers and companies financing AI infrastructure were among the session's biggest losers. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4%, while Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) dropped 2.9%, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) slid 3.9%, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) lost 4.8%.
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) declined 4.4%, and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) shed 5.5%, amid concerns about the financing required to support large-scale AI infrastructure projects.
Investors were also monitoring oil prices amid heightened concerns about Middle East supply disruptions. U.S. crude futures settled 3.6% higher, while Brent crude rose 4.1% above $104 per barrel, adding to inflation concerns at a time when borrowing costs remain elevated.
Hurricane-related production cuts in the Gulf of Mexico further tightened supply expectations.
Treasury yields retreated from their session highs after a $22 billion auction of 30-year bonds drew steady demand, providing some relief to bond markets.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell to around 5.23%, after earlier climbing to levels near its highest since 2002. However, elevated yields continued to weigh on the appeal of growth stocks, whose valuations are particularly sensitive to borrowing costs.
Investors are now looking ahead to the start of the third-quarter earnings season next week, when major U.S. banks are due to report results.

title: Meta bans TikTok ads on its platforms in US
full_text:

By Rishabh Jaiswal and Mrinmay Dey
Oct 8 (Reuters) - Facebook and Instagram-owner Meta has banned advertisements by ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, on its platforms in the United States and a handful of other countries, a company spokesperson said on Thursday.
The move marks an escalation in the long-running rivalry between Meta and ByteDance, whose video-sharing app TikTok has emerged as one of Meta’s most formidable competitors for user engagement, creators and advertising dollars.
Meta’s ban takes effect immediately in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, and extends to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries, Meta said.
"We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta said. "Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience."
TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Meta’s move.
TikTok’s website shows that it does not support links that open or log users into other social media apps. However, users can still add links to their profiles that direct people to those platforms’ websites.
Meta has been urging TikTok and YouTube to follow steps it agreed to take on teen safety in August following a settlement of up to $18 billion with US states over social media harms to children.
Meta in August agreed to impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.
TikTok has not publicly commented on Meta’s campaign, but it reached a settlement with Alabama in September that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhance age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that it endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.
TikTok operates in the US as a majority American-owned joint venture after a deal aimed at safeguarding US user data and averting a US ban on an app used by more than 200 million users in the country.
Bloomberg News first reported Meta’s ban earlier on Thursday.

title: China defends yuan policy as Europe steps up pressure over trade surplus
full_text:

By Yukun Zhang and Kevin Yao
BEIJING, Oct 8 (Reuters) - China pushed back against foreign criticism of its exchange-rate policy on Thursday, saying it has never pursued competitive depreciation, as European policymakers call for a stronger yuan to help curb China’s record trade surplus and export surge.
As China’s trade surplus swells, European leaders have intensified calls for a stronger yuan, fearing a "China Shock 2.0" from a fresh wave of Chinese exports.
In a lengthy policy statement, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) rejected claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage, as the EU’s trade chief Maros Sefcovic is in Beijing to discuss narrowing the bloc’s trade deficit with China.
"China neither needs nor intends to obtain a trade-competitive advantage through exchange-rate depreciation, and has never engaged in competitive currency depreciation," the central bank said.
"Attributing a decline in domestic industrial competitiveness, the weakening of fiscal and financial discipline and complex structural problems simply to the exchange rates of other nations amounts to evading and shirking one’s own responsibility for making necessary adjustments."
China posted a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025, equivalent to about 6% of GDP, with analysts expecting exports of AI-related and other advanced technology products to help keep the surplus elevated this year.
China’s trade strength stems from the global competitiveness of its industries, the central bank said, arguing that countries with large trade surpluses have historically been those with strong manufacturing sectors.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde in June urged global leaders to discuss undervaluation of the Chinese currency as a facet of the imbalances endangering the global economy. The bloc is concerned about its trade imbalance with China, which reached €360.6 billion ($404 billion) in 2025, according to EU data, up 15% from the previous year.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said the yuan is undervalued by 25% to 30% and called for a dialogue with China on monetary policy.
Goldman Sachs said in August that the yuan is undervalued by at least 20% on some of its valuation models, arguing that a stronger currency would help narrow China’s outsized trade and current-account surpluses and ease protectionist pressure from trading partners.
The PBOC said exchange rates reflect multiple economic and financial factors, rejecting claims that isolated model estimates prove the yuan is undervalued.
CHINA SAYS MARKET PLAYS DECISIVE ROLE
The yuan has climbed about 4% against the dollar this year despite a widening US-China yield gap.
The PBOC said the yuan has appreciated about 23% against the dollar since China’s 2005 exchange-rate reform, strengthening from 8.27 yuan per dollar to around 6.7 currently.
It warned that the yuan’s outlook remains uncertain, with forces for both appreciation and depreciation shaping its trajectory.
China lets the market play a decisive role in exchange-rate formation, the central bank said, adding that it does not preset exchange rate target levels or intervene in long-term exchange rate trends.
"The People’s Bank of China does not preset an exchange-rate target level, does not intervene in the long-term trend of the exchange rate, and maintains exchange-rate flexibility and two-way movement," it said.
China will report additional foreign exchange-related data to the International Monetary Fund starting from 2027, the central bank said.
The PBOC said China would pursue a domestic demand-led growth model under its 2026-2030 plan, boosting consumption, expanding effective investment and deepening high-level opening-up, while strengthening the domestic economy and helping drive a more balanced global economy.

2. OpenAI expects annualized revenues to reach $70 billion by end-2026 - Bloomberg News
However, Nasdaq 100 futures were buoyed this morning by a Bloomberg News report which said OpenAI expects to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year.

Annualized revenues are a critical metric for AI startups like OpenAI and rival Anthropic. The measures are used to gauge overall AI demand and the need for more computing infrastructure.

On a relatively sparse earnings calendar, markets will be keeping tabs on returns from carrier Delta Air Lines before the opening bell.
For the third quarter, Delta is seen posting adjusted revenue of $17.66 billion and adjusted per-share income of $1.82, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.
In July, Delta reiterated its full-year profit outlook and issued stronger-than-anticipated third-quarter guidance, underlining that it expects to maintain fare increases connected to a recent spike in fuel costs.

Year-ahead inflation expectations in September jumped to the highest since June.
Overall, last month’s study revealed "broad agreement across the political spectrum" that the outlook for the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year.

U.S. mobile tower stocks rose in extended hours trading after SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) agreed to buy a nationwide block of low-band spectrum, which Bernstein said keeps alive the possibility that the satellite company builds a ground network.

The acquisition is aimed at improving SpaceX’s Starlink satellite-to-cellular service, with the new spectrum allowing its signal to pass through obstacles– which was a major hurdle for the service.
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said.

By Rajesh Kumar Singh
CHICAGO, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Delta Air Lines cut its annual profit forecast by nearly a quarter on Friday, as surging fuel costs, expected to add $6 billion to its bill in 2026, overwhelmed resilient travel demand and higher ticket prices.
Its shares fell 3.5% in premarket trading after the carrier cut its 2026 profit forecast for the first time this year and lifted its projected fuel-cost increase by $2 billion as the Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher worldwide. With no end to the war in sight, carriers are confronting their worst crisis since the pandemic.
The downgrade underscores a growing challenge for the industry: whether passengers will absorb further fare increases if fuel prices remain elevated. Airlines have already raised fares substantially this year, and analysts warn further increases could test travelers’ willingness to keep spending.
Delta, the first major global carrier to report third-quarter results, said fuel expenses for the period rose 62% from a year earlier to $4.1 billion, exceeding its July forecast by more than $500 million.
"All of it’s fuel," Delta Chief Financial Officer Erik Snell told reporters when asked what drove the forecast cut, citing increases in both
crude oil and refined jet fuel prices since the summer.
Delta now expects adjusted annual earnings of $5.10 to $5.60 a share, down from the $6.50 to $7.50 it forecast in July. The new midpoint of $5.35 is below analysts’ average estimate of $5.46, according to LSEG. It forecast $4.5 billion in adjusted pre-tax profit for 2026.
Third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.72 a share narrowly missed analysts’ average estimate of $1.76, according to LSEG. Its adjusted operating margin fell to 9.4% from 11.1%.
Rivals United Airlines, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines are due to report later this month. Ryanair Group CEO Michael O’Leary warned on Thursday that European airlines could face more than another year of elevated fuel costs due to the war.
HIGHER FARES
US airlines spent $42.9 billion on fuel for scheduled flights in the first eight months of 2026, nearly $13.2 billion more than a year earlier, despite using slightly less fuel, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
Strong demand and limited growth in seats have helped carriers pass higher fuel costs on to passengers. US airline fares rose an average of about 25% from a year earlier in the five months through August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index.
With fuel prices remaining elevated and planned industry capacity growth set to accelerate in the fourth quarter from the third, analysts are watching whether carriers, including Delta, can raise fares further without discouraging travel.
Deutsche Bank analysts expect the industry to recover a smaller share of higher fuel costs through revenue measures in the fourth quarter, with full recovery not expected until early 2027.
Delta said demand remains strong. With almost 60% of the fourth quarter already booked, it expects revenue growth of about 20% from a year ago, Snell said.
It forecast fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.15 to $1.65 a share, with the $1.40 midpoint roughly in line with analysts’ average estimate of $1.39, according to LSEG.
REFINERY ADVANTAGE
Delta has an advantage over other major US airlines: its ownership of a refinery outside Philadelphia that Snell expects to generate $700 million in profit this year.
"We have a refinery that gives us an offset, a partial offset to fuel prices that no one else does," he said.
Bought in 2012, the Monroe refinery processes crude oil into jet fuel and other products. Delta still pays market prices for fuel transferred to its airline operations, but retains the refining profit within the company.
That helps when the gap between crude and refined fuel prices widens, increasing costs for airlines buying from outside suppliers. The protection varies with refining margins, however, and the refinery can lose money when those margins weaken.
But the refinery can only partly cushion the impact of higher fuel prices. Even with a projected refinery benefit of 40 cents a gallon, Delta expects its fuel cost to rise to $4.25 a gallon in the fourth quarter from $3.61 in the third.
Snell said fuel costs were expected to stay elevated for some time.
"Ultimately, fuel will come down. When that is, we’re not exactly sure," he said.

The hurricane was moving east-northeast at 10 mph (17 kph), about 355 miles (570 km) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River at 1 p.m. US Central time, the NHC said.
IMPACTS ON OIL, GAS
The Marine Minerals Administration, which monitors offshore US oil and gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico, said on Thursday that personnel have been evacuated from 121 production platforms and five non-dynamically positioned rigs ahead of the storm.
About 63% of current oil production in the Gulf, or 1.3 million barrels of oil a day, has been shut in, the agency said, citing operator reports. Just over 1.1 billion cubic feet a day of natural gas production has also been shut in, or about 57% of total output from the region.
On Wednesday, 25% of oil production and 16% of natural gas output had been shut in.
About 9 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates.
The companies with the most exposure to the storm include BP, Chevron, ENI, Murphy Oil and Shell, among others, according to the Earth Science model.
WARNINGS, STORM SURGE
Hurricane warnings stretched from coastal Mississippi through Alabama to the Florida panhandle, while tropical-storm and storm-surge warnings extended into southeastern Louisiana, the NHC said.
Forecasters warned that storm surges could reach 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2.1 meters) above sea level in the hardest-hit coastal areas, with rainfall of 3 to 7 inches (8 to 18 cm) and isolated totals of 15 inches (38 cm).
The hurricane was forecast to weaken somewhat as it approached land. Increasing vertical wind shear, which can disrupt a hurricane’s circulation, was expected to limit its strength near landfall, though forecasters warned it would remain dangerous.
EVACUATIONS ORDERED
In Florida, officials ordered mandatory evacuations beginning at noon local time on Thursday for coastal areas of Okaloosa County.
The county urged tourists to leave the area and announced plans to close three airports Thursday evening. Governor Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in 25 Florida counties earlier in the week.
Alabama Governor Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency covering 40 counties, while officials on Dauphin Island issued an evacuation notice for the western portion of the barrier island beginning Thursday evening.
Baldwin County, Alabama, encouraged residents of low-lying coastal areas to evacuate voluntarily and prepared emergency shelters.
In Mississippi, Jackson County and the city of Gautier declared local emergencies as coastal communities prepared for flooding and power outages.

title: UAW President Shawn Fain declares victory in race for second term
full_text:
Wall Street ends higher, Nasdaq and Dow post weekly gains as oil eases
By Kalea Hall
DETROIT, Oct 9 (Reuters) - United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain declared victory on Friday in a race to maintain his position as head of the 400,000-member union.
Fain, 57, who rose to national prominence during a 2023 strike against General Motors, Ford and Chrysler-parent Stellantis, received a majority of the votes and easily topped five challengers, according to preliminary ballot totals released by a federal monitor overseeing the vote.
Fain had widely been expected to win the balloting, which the Detroit Three automakers were watching closely as they look ahead to 2028 contract negotiations. The companies are wary of raising their labor costs at a time when the auto industry is grappling with weaker vehicle demand and intensifying competition.
“One thing I know about our membership is they’re ready to fight,” Fain said in an interview with Reuters. “They know they deserve better. And let’s not fool ourselves. All these companies are massively profitable.”
Fain has pointed to the next round of negotiations as an opportunity to secure gains beyond the union’s landmark 2023 contract, which delivered wage increases of more than 25% over the four-year life of the agreement. The UAW is already urging members to strike in the spring of 2028, when current contracts with the Detroit automakers expire.
GM, Ford and Stellantis did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Fain’s declared victory late Friday.
FAIN’S COMBATIVE APPROACH LED TO GAINS
In 2023, just months after narrowly winning his seat, Fain took an unorthodox, combative stance against the automakers.
He insisted on bargaining with all three automakers at once, a departure from past practice, in which the union got an agreement at one company to use as a template for the other two. Eventually, he launched simultaneous strikes at factories across all three automakers, a first for the union.
“Shawn Fain will continue to take an aggressive approach to collective bargaining. The challenge this time will be that the companies will be well aware” of that approach, said Stephen Silvia, a labor expert from American University.
DETROIT AUTOMAKERS LEERY OF LABOR-COST INCREASES
Fain said on Friday that in 2028 he plans to push to restore pensions for all workers, a benefit that ended for new hires in 2007, around the time of the near-collapse of domestic US auto companies.
GM, Ford and Stellantis, meanwhile, have been stung by tariff expenses, higher raw-materials costs and an expensive rollback of their electric-vehicle plans amid weak US demand. Executives are likely to push back against any meaningful labor-cost increases, said Marick Masters, business professor emeritus at Detroit’s Wayne State University.
“The recipe is there for a major confrontation with the companies being in a less favorable position to withstand the pressures,” he said.

title: Trump takes suit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
full_text:
Wall Street ends higher, Nasdaq and Dow post weekly gains as oil eases
By Andrew Chung
Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year’s election by linking his campaign to Russia.
The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.
In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.
Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims.
Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.
US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax."
Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year’s election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.
’POLITICAL MANIFESTO’
US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump’s lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump’s lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him."
Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and his lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts."
Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories.
The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge’s rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.
"Many of Trump’s and Habba’s legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated.
In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the decisions by the lower courts are having a "profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole."
Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion," but stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities."
Mueller said in his report that he found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia’s effort to tilt the ballot in Trump’s favor.
Trump’s then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential missteps by the FBI.
In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump’s political opponents to fuel the probe.
Trump’s Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.
Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump’s campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, all of which Trump denied.

The new Alexa Tablets incorporate Alexa+, the company’s upgraded voice assistant powered by generative artificial intelligence.
Amazon spent several years developing Alexa+ to handle longer, more complex user requests as it seeks to improve the capabilities of its voice assistant.

Alexa has consistently generated losses for Amazon since its introduction in 2014, making the company’s push into AI-powered devices a significant part of its efforts to develop the business.

Kalshi’s market had assigned her approximately a 1% probability of securing the role in the days preceding the announcement.
President Trump confirmed Zacharia’s appointment in a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon. The White House did not respond to the WSJ’s request for comment.
The investigation comes amid growing scrutiny of prediction markets and concerns that individuals with access to confidential government information could profit from wagers on political developments.
Trump’s former teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez, was previously dismissed after earning more than $100,000 from bets involving the president’s speeches. Perez settled with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in August.
The White House also previously warned staff against using nonpublic information for personal financial gain following suspicious wagers linked to the Iran war.
Kalshi maintains identifying records of traders, although individual trading activity remains anonymous to the public.
